lesson.title: The Number Line: Turning Order Into a Picture
lesson.summary: The number line is the one-axis ancestor of the coordinate system, converting the abstract ideas of order and distance between numbers into positions and lengths you can see and measure.
lesson.body:
A coordinate system assigns pairs of numbers to points in a plane, but its single-axis ancestor, the number line, is simpler and arguably more fundamental: it assigns one number to each point along a single line, turning the abstract idea of "bigger than" or "smaller than" into something you can literally see as "further right" or "further left." Every number line has three ingredients: a starting point called the origin, usually labeled 0, a direction of increase (traditionally rightward), and a fixed unit length that marks off 1, 2, 3, and so on, along with their negatives on the other side.

The power of the number line is that it converts two different kinds of questions, order and distance, into geometry. Order becomes left-right position: a < b means a sits to the left of b. Distance becomes length: the distance between two numbers a and b is |a - b|, the length of the segment joining them, which is always nonnegative no matter which number is larger. This is exactly the one-dimensional version of the distance idea used in a full coordinate system, just without a second axis to worry about.

The number line also gives a natural picture for solving inequalities. Consider |x - 3| < 2. In words, this says "the distance from x to 3 is less than 2 units." Picture 3 on the number line, then mark off 2 units in each direction: that lands you at 1 and at 5. Every point strictly between those two boundaries satisfies the inequality, so the solution is the interval 1 < x < 5. You can check this algebraically too: |x - 3| < 2 is equivalent to -2 < x - 3 < 2, and adding 3 across all three parts gives 1 < x < 5, matching the picture exactly.

It's worth verifying with actual numbers. Try x = 4: |4 - 3| = 1, and 1 < 2, so x = 4 is a solution, consistent with 4 lying inside (1, 5). Try x = 6: |6 - 3| = 3, and 3 is not less than 2, so x = 6 is not a solution, consistent with 6 lying outside the interval.

This interval, all x with 1 < x < 5, is usually written in interval notation as (1, 5), with parentheses signaling that the endpoints themselves, 1 and 5, are not included, since the inequality was strict. Had the original problem instead been |x - 3| <= 2, meaning "less than or equal to," the endpoints would be included and the answer would be written as the closed interval [1, 5], with square brackets. This bracket-versus-parenthesis distinction is really just a notational shorthand for a fact the number line already shows directly: whether the boundary points themselves belong to the shaded region or merely mark where it stops.

This geometric way of thinking about order and distance is the quiet backbone of almost everything that follows in calculus. When you later say a function value gets "close to" some number, or that x is "near" some point a, you are making a number-line statement about distance, |x - a| being small, dressed up in calculus language.
